subject: social_science
chapter_title: Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age

concepts.title: Shifting Cultivation (Jhum)
concepts.definition: A traditional farming method where small forest plots are cleared by cutting treetops and burning vegetation to enrich the soil with potash-rich ash before scattering seeds.
concepts.key_idea: Cultivating a plot temporarily and leaving it fallow for years to restore soil fertility naturally.
question_patterns: What is shifting cultivation or jhum cultivation?
How did jhum cultivators prepare their land for farming?
Why was ash spread on the fields in shifting cultivation?
Where was shifting cultivation primarily practiced in India?
Explain the process of jhum cultivation in forest tracts.

solution_steps.explain: Cultivators cut treetops for sunlight and burnt vegetation to clear the ground.
They spread potash-containing ash from the fire to fertilize the soil.
They scattered seeds instead of ploughing, and moved to a new field once the crop was harvested, leaving the old field fallow.

concepts.title: Hunters and Gatherers
concepts.definition: Tribal communities that sustained themselves by collectively hunting wild animals and gathering forest produce like fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
concepts.key_idea: Complete reliance on forest resources for food, medicine, and local trade.
question_patterns: How did the Khonds of Orissa sustain themselves?
What forest products did hunter-gatherers use for food and medicine?
Why were local weavers and leather workers dependent on the Khonds?
Describe the lifestyle of hunter-gatherer tribal groups.
How did forest communities obtain grains and other essential goods?

solution_steps.explain: They ate forest fruits, roots, and meat from collective hunts, cooking with oil from sal and mahua seeds.
They sold forest produce in local markets and exchanged valuable forest items for grains.
They supplied kusum and palash flowers to local weavers and leather workers for coloring clothes.

concepts.title: Pastoralist Herders
concepts.definition: Nomadic tribal groups who reared livestock and migrated seasonally across different geographical regions in search of fresh pastures.
concepts.key_idea: Seasonal migration with herds of cattle, sheep, or goats based on grass availability.
question_patterns: Who were the pastoralist tribal groups mentioned in the text?
How did herders adjust their movements according to the seasons?
Name the cattle herders of the Punjab hills and Andhra Pradesh.
Which tribal group in Kashmir was known for rearing goats?
Describe the seasonal movement of the Gaddis of Kulu.

solution_steps.explain: Pastoralists moved with their herds of cattle or sheep according to seasonal changes.
Van Gujjars (Punjab hills) and Labadis (Andhra Pradesh) herded cattle; Gaddis (Kulu) were shepherds; Bakarwals (Kashmir) reared goats.

concepts.title: Settled Cultivation
concepts.definition: A system where tribal communities abandoned nomadic farming to cultivate fixed plots of land continuously, often using ploughs and establishing clan-based land rights.
concepts.key_idea: Transition from shifting to permanent agriculture with defined land rights.
question_patterns: How did settled cultivation differ from shifting cultivation?
What were the land rights of the Mundas of Chottanagpur?
Why did British officials prefer settled tribal groups over shifting cultivators?
How did power dynamics change within clans practicing settled agriculture?
Which tribal groups were viewed as more civilized by the British?

solution_steps.explain: Land belonged to the clan as a whole, with all members regarded as descendants of the original settlers.
They used ploughs and cultivated the same fields year after year instead of moving.
British officials saw settled groups like Gonds and Santhals as more civilized than wild forest-dwelling hunter-gatherers.

concepts.title: Impact of Colonial Rule on Tribal Chiefs
concepts.definition: The administrative and economic transformation under British rule where traditional leaders lost their sovereign authority, police powers, and administrative control, becoming mere rent collectors and tribute payers.
concepts.key_idea: Loss of traditional administrative authority and subordination to British laws.
question_patterns: How did the powers of tribal chiefs change under British rule?
What administrative functions did tribal chiefs lose during colonial administration?
Were tribal chiefs allowed to keep their land titles under the British?
Why were tribal chiefs unable to fulfill their traditional roles under colonial rule?
Explain the impact of British policies on traditional tribal leadership.

solution_steps.explain: Chiefs kept land titles over clusters of villages and could rent out land.
They lost administrative power, were forced to follow British laws, and had to pay tribute to the colonial state.

concepts.title: Forest Laws and Reserved Forests
concepts.definition: Colonial regulations that declared forests as state property and restricted tribal access to resources, classifying key timber-producing areas to secure raw materials for railway sleepers.
concepts.key_idea: State control of forests leading to loss of tribal livelihoods and creation of forest villages for cheap labor.
question_patterns: What were Reserved Forests and why did the British establish them?
How did changes in forest laws affect the lives of shifting cultivators?
Why did the British establish forest villages in tribal areas?
What was the purpose of railway sleepers and how did it impact forests?
How did tribal groups react to colonial forest laws?

solution_steps.explain: Forests controlled by the state to produce timber for British needs, where free movement and jhum cultivation were banned.
Banning tribals left the Forest Department without labor to cut trees for railway sleepers.
The British set up forest villages, giving small land patches to jhum cultivators in exchange for cheap labor.

concepts.title: Middleman Price Markup in Silk Trade
concepts.definition: The calculation of the export price of silk cocoons based on the purchase price paid to tribal growers and the multiplier markup charged by middlemen.
concepts.key_idea: Middlemen sold cocoons at a multiple of the price they paid to Santhal weavers.
question_patterns: If Santhal growers are paid {purchase_price} rupees for cocoons and the middlemen sell them at a markup of {markup_factor} times, what is the export price?
Calculate the export price of cocoons when the buying price is {purchase_price} and the resale multiplier is {markup_factor}.
Find the final selling price of silk cocoons bought at {purchase_price} rupees with a markup factor of {markup_factor}.
How much did the middlemen sell the cocoons for in Gaya if they bought them for {purchase_price} rupees and marked them up by {markup_factor} times?
What is the export value of a batch of cocoons purchased at {purchase_price} rupees and sold at a {markup_factor} fold price?

solution_steps.action: Identify the purchase price paid to the tribal growers
solution_steps.explain: The buying price is represented by purchase_price.

solution_steps.action: Multiply the purchase price by the markup factor to find the export price
solution_steps.explain: The export price is the product of the purchase price and the markup factor.

concepts.title: Tribal Rebellions
concepts.definition: Armed uprisings and resistance movements organized by various tribal communities across India against colonial forest laws, high taxes, and exploitation by traders.
concepts.key_idea: Active resistance to British policies and economic exploitation through organized revolts.
question_patterns: When did the Kols rebel against colonial policies?
What was the significance of the Santhal revolt of 1855?
Where and when did the Bastar Rebellion take place?
Name some of the major tribal uprisings during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
Why did tribal groups rise in open rebellion against the British and dikus?

solution_steps.explain: Kols rebelled in 1831-32; Santhals rose in 1855; Bastar Rebellion occurred in 1910; Warli Revolt happened in 1940.
Tribals rebelled against changes in laws, restrictions on traditional practices, new taxes, and exploitation by traders and moneylenders.

concepts.title: Birsa Munda and the Golden Age
concepts.definition: A socio-religious and political movement led by Birsa Munda aiming to reform tribal society, resist colonial land policies, and restore a legendary era of self-rule and purity.
concepts.key_idea: Restoration of ancestral rights and establishment of a Munda Raj free from dikus.
question_patterns: What was Birsa Munda's vision of a golden age or satyug?
How did Birsa Munda urge his followers to reform their society?
Why did the political aims of the Birsa movement worry British officials?
What was the significance of the Birsa Munda movement?
How did Birsa Munda use traditional symbols to gather support?

solution_steps.explain: Birsa envisioned a golden age where Mundas lived honestly, built embankments, planted orchards, and did not kill their relatives.
He urged followers to clean their villages, stop drinking liquor, and reject belief in witchcraft and sorcery.
The movement aimed to set up a Munda Raj by driving out missionaries, landlords, and the British government, forcing the introduction of protective land laws.
